Low-income entry and exit rates use different starting groups: read the people behind the percentages

Five charts connect Canadian low-income transition rates with their denominators, person counts and within-pair flows, then build a separate household cash-gap example.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read a historical transition pair beside a separate cash-gap example

Interactive planning lab

The first four charts use 55 public observations for five two-year transition pairs, 2018/2019 through 2022/2023. Canada here covers tax filers age 18+ in the ten provinces who filed in both years, Both sexes, Variable low income measure (LIM). Percentages and person counts are different units. Each pair has its own matched filer population; the five pairs are not one fixed long-term cohort. The final cash chart uses only the three hypothetical budget inputs and does not convert a national transition rate into a personal forecast. No cause of income change, job-loss probability, duration forecast or recommended reserve is inferred.

The central idea

An entry rate and an exit rate cannot be directly subtracted to find the change in people. Reconcile the starting populations and flows, then use actual household dollars for a reserve plan.

01

A percentage needs the population that could make the transition

Between 2022 and 2023, the selected Canadian statistics show a 4.1% low-income entry rate and a 34.9% exit rate. Those percentages start with different groups. Entry concerns tax filers who were initially outside low income; exit concerns tax filers who were initially in low income.

Subtracting 4.1 from 34.9 produces a 30.8-percentage-point difference between two conditional rates. It does not measure the percentage-point change in the overall low-income share, the number of people leaving minus entering or a household’s chance of recovering income.

The charts use Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0024-01, selecting Canada, Both sexes and the Variable low income measure. They retain the first and second years of each transition pair rather than treating the observation as a single-year level.

02

Identify the tax-filer population and the low-income definition

This table’s Canada selection covers tax filers aged at least 18 in the ten provinces who filed in both years. It is not a count of every Canadian resident, child or household. The measure uses census-family after-tax income adjusted by the square root of family size, with a threshold based on half the median adjusted income.

The variable threshold is re-estimated each year. It differs from the table’s separate measure fixed in 2002 and subsequently price-adjusted. The charts use only the variable measure, so those two definitions are never spliced together.

Statistics Canada’s Dimensions of Poverty Hub distinguishes these Low Income Measure transitions from Canada’s official poverty measure based on the Market Basket Measure. A move across the selected statistical threshold is not, by itself, a full account of a person’s living costs or financial security.

03

Use the person counts to reconstruct the two denominators

The 2022/2023 matched population contains 28,303,440 tax filers. Of these, 4,439,745 were initially in low income. The initial non-low-income group is the difference: 23,863,695.

There were 980,895 entrants. Dividing that count by 23,863,695 gives about 4.1104%, which rounds to the published 4.1%. There were 1,549,805 exits. Dividing by 4,439,745 gives about 34.9075%, which rounds to 34.9%.

The larger exit percentage therefore does not mean applying 34.9% to the much larger non-low-income group. The grouped chart places each actual transition count beside its own eligible starting group. All bars in that figure measure people.

04

Keep the four possible start-to-end states visible

The count matrix records two statuses in the first year and two in the second. For 2022/2023, 2,889,940 tax filers remained in low income, 1,549,805 exited, 980,895 entered and 22,882,800 were outside low income in both years.

Adding the two cells in the first row reconstructs the initial low-income count. Adding the two cells in the first column reconstructs the later low-income count. Adding all four cells reconstructs the entire matched population.

Cell counts and conditional rates are different views of the same selected pair. Normalising each row would produce row-based transition percentages; dividing by the entire population would instead produce population shares. The chart displays counts, with that denominator choice left explicit.

05

Reconcile the change with entrants and exits measured in people

The within-pair waterfall follows a count identity: 4,439,745 initially low income + 980,895 entrants − 1,549,805 exits = 3,870,835 low income in the second year.

The decrease in the low-income count within this matched pair is therefore 568,910. If a change in the matched-population share is wanted, divide that person-count change by the same 28,303,440 denominator. Directly subtracting the published entry and exit rates cannot perform that calculation.

The bridge reports a descriptive reconciliation. It does not establish why a person’s status changed, attribute a movement to a policy or estimate how long a later income interruption might last. Those questions need additional evidence.

06

Adjacent transition pairs do not create one fixed panel

The historical line shows five pairs, from 2018/2019 through 2022/2023. Every pair requires qualifying tax returns in both of its years. The participating population can change between pairs.

For that reason, the second-year low-income count in the 2021/2022 pair need not equal the first-year count in the 2022/2023 pair, even though both labels refer to 2022. Joining them without checking coverage would erase the difference between two matched populations.

The article’s source check preserves each pair’s original values. It verifies all four transition cells, both low-income counts, the total matched count and the four rates. It does not force adjacent pairs into an artificial single cohort or claim that the same people contribute to every plotted point.

07

Build the household reserve from its own cash gap

The final chart asks a separate planning question. Suppose essential expenses are CAD 2,500 a month, cash available for them is CAD 2,100 and starting reserve is CAD 2,400. The selected shortfall is CAD 400 per month.

Using that reserve for a constant month-end gap leaves CAD 2,000 after one month, CAD 1,200 after three and zero after six. At month seven, the cumulative amount not funded by the initial reserve reaches CAD 400. At month twelve it reaches CAD 2,400.

No national entry or exit percentage is multiplied into these cash figures. Changing the historical year changes the source snapshot; it leaves the household scenario intact. Changing expenses, receipts or reserve changes the cash chart without rewriting the official observations.

08

Keep the statistical question beside the financial-planning question

The statistics describe movement across a particular income threshold among a particular tax-filer population. The cash example describes a selected household shortfall. They can inform different parts of a planning discussion while retaining their separate units and evidence.

A real reserve review also needs payment dates, other expenses, support eligibility, insurance, access to savings and the capacity to rebuild money after use. Income changes can be irregular, and an annual threshold transition does not supply a monthly receipt calendar.

  1. Read the population, income measure and two-year reference pair.
  2. Match every conditional percentage to its starting group.
  3. Use person counts for a flow reconciliation.
  4. Check whether a comparison follows the same matched population.
  5. Use actual household costs and cash dates to build a reserve scenario.

The latest pair in this downloaded table is 2022/2023. Its retrieval date is 25 October 2026; that retrieval does not turn the historical observations into current household conditions or a forecast.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four charts use 55 official observations from Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0024-01, 31 October 2025 release, retrieved 25 October 2026. The fifth chart is an independent hypothetical cash example. National transition rates are never used as personal probabilities. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Table 11-10-0024-01 · Low income entry and exit rates of tax filers in Canada ↗

    Released 31 October 2025; original public CSV and metadata retrieved 25 October 2026. Selects Canada, Both sexes, Variable low income measure, 2018/2019–2022/2023: 55 observations, 11 measures in each of five pairs. Rates are published to one decimal place; counts are persons in units. All selected values are present and unflagged. Count identities reconcile exactly in this slice. Adapted from Statistics Canada, Table 11-10-0024-01. This does not constitute an endorsement by Statistics Canada of this product.

  2. Statistics Canada · Dimensions of Poverty Hub · Low income entry and exit rates ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for entry/exit denominator definitions, the distinction from the official poverty-line indicator and publication coverage. The hub states that 2023/2024 transitions are expected in spring 2027. Its rounded headline person totals are not substituted for the original CSV counts used here.

  3. Statistics Canada · Open Licence ↗

    Public Statistics Canada information is adapted with source acknowledgement. The original cash example, chart design, subtraction and denominator reconstructions are TickerLantern calculations. No private tax return, account record or identifiable person is used.
